12	## 1. Known defects
13	
14	None of these are fixed. Each is reachable from the current code unless noted.
15	
16	### D1 — `ReportModal.View()` emits invalid UTF-8
17	
18	`internal/ui/components/report_modal.go:136-139`
19	
20	Long entries are truncated with `item[len(item)-52:]`, which slices **bytes**, not
21	runes. When the resulting offset falls inside a multi-byte codepoint the rendered
22	output is no longer valid UTF-8 and the terminal shows replacement characters.
23	
24	Reachable with any non-ASCII repository path. Pinned by
25	`TestReportModalViewTruncationSplitsMultibyteRunes`, which `t.Skip()`s with
26	instructions once the truncation becomes rune-aware.
27	
28	**Fix:** truncate on `[]rune`, and measure width with `runewidth` rather than
29	`len()`.
30	
31	### D2 — The "permanent delete" checkbox is documented as locked but is not
32	
33	`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:35` and `:99-105`
34	
35	`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent` pre-checks *Immediate deletion* and its doc
36	comment states the box is non-modifiable ("pré-cochée et non modifiable"). Nothing
37	enforces that: `space` and `enter` on the checkbox still toggle it.
38	
39	A project already marked for deletion can therefore be sent through a
40	grace-period delete that the caller does not expect. Pinned by
41	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable`.
42	
43	**Fix:** carry a `locked` flag on the modal and make the toggle a no-op when set,
44	or drop the claim from the doc comment.
45	
46	### D3 — `wrapInputLines` loops forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`
47	
48	`internal/ui/components/wrapped_input.go:135`
49	
50	With a non-positive wrap width the loop makes no progress: `breakAt` collapses to
51	`start`, an empty line is appended, and `start` never advances — the line slice
52	grows until the process runs out of memory.
53	
54	**Not reachable today.** Every caller passes 60, 80 or 100 per Rule 133. Latent
55	only, which is why no test covers it (the test would hang).
56	
57	**Fix:** guard the entry point — return a single line when `wrapWidth < 1`.
58	
59	### D4 — `DeleteConfirmModal` uses `Tab` for field navigation
60	
61	`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:89-97`
62	
63	`tab` / `shift+tab` cycle checkbox → Yes → No. Rule 135 reserves those keys for
64	tab switching and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively.
65	
66	Cosmetic in isolation, but it is the kind of inconsistency Rule 135 exists to
67	prevent. Changing it alters muscle memory, so it needs a deliberate call rather
68	than a drive-by fix.
69	
70	### D5 — Unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`
71	
72	`internal/ui/components/creation_form.go:221-223`
73	
74	After cycling the resource type, the code clamps `focusedField` down to
75	`maxField()`. The surrounding branch only runs when `focusedField == 0`, and
76	`maxField()` is never below 4, so the clamp can never fire.
77	
78	Dead defensive code. Harmless, but it implies a state transition that cannot
79	happen and is misleading to read.
80	
81	### D6 — `wordWrap` measures bytes, not runes
82	
83	`internal/ui/help/help.go:123`
84	
85	Word widths come from `len(word)`, which counts bytes. Accented text therefore
86	wraps earlier than its rendered width requires: two 5-rune words occupy 11
87	columns but 21 bytes, so a width of 12 splits them apart.
88	
89	Low impact today — Rule 129 keeps help content in English US — but it is the same
90	byte-vs-rune class as [D1](#d1--reportmodalview-emits-invalid-utf-8). Unlike
91	[D3](#d3--wrapinputlines-loops-forever-when-wrapwidth--0), `wordWrap` does guard
92	a non-positive width, and that guard is covered by a test so it does not get
93	"tidied" away.
94	
95	Pinned by `TestWordWrapMeasuresBytesNotRunes`.
96	
97	**Fix:** measure with `utf8.RuneCountInString`, or `runewidth.StringWidth` if
98	double-width glyphs ever appear.
99	
100	### D7 — `extractTarGz` keeps parent references in archive paths
101	
102	`internal/oci/oci.go:262`
103	
104	Extraction strips leading `./` and `/` but does not reject `..`, so an archive
105	member named `../../etc/passwd` survives as a map key containing parent
106	references.
107	
108	**Not exploitable today.** The sole consumer, `applyTemplate` in
109	`internal/ui/gitlab/explorer/model.go:1053`, turns the map into GitLab commit
110	actions rather than writing to disk, and the server validates the paths.
111	
112	Recorded because the hazard is latent: any future caller that writes these keys

Le backlog est à jour (`docs/backlog.md`, rien de nouveau depuis le rename du module en #4). J'ai vérifié la couverture réelle — elle correspond aux chiffres du doc.

## La suite immédiate : finir la phase 1 de la couverture

C'est la seule ligne du backlog explicitement « en cours ». Restent trois packages (~255 statements) :

| Package | Actuel | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/gitlab` | **7.5 %** | le plus gros gain ; client API, à tester via `httptest` |
| `internal/credentials` | **29.5 %** | `FileStorage` / `MemoryStorage` testables directement, `GitCredentialStorage` demande un seam d'exec |
| `internal/ui/theme` | **78.9 %** | complément (helpers `Bg`/`PadWithBg`/`TimeAgo`, `TableStylesFor*`) |

Un package n'apparaît dans aucune phase du plan : **`internal/registrymgr` à 18.5 %**. Oubli à corriger dans le tableau.

## Ensuite, un arbitrage à trancher avant la phase 2

Le backlog le signale mais ne le résout pas : les vues de la phase 2/3 (`security/model.go` 1785 lignes, `oci_resources/update.go` 1556, `app.go` 1333…) dépassent le plafond de 800 lignes. Écrire quelques milliers de statements de tests contre elles **fige leur structure actuelle**. Deux ordres possibles :

1. **Découper d'abord** — plus lent à démarrer, mais les tests écrits ensuite restent valides.
2. **Tester d'abord** — filet de sécurité pour le découpage, mais tests à réécrire après.

Mon avis : découper d'abord `internal/docker/client.go`, parce qu'il est de toute façon bloquant — la phase 5 ne peut pas commencer sans un seam d'exécution injectable (il `exec` le CLI Docker en direct). Ce refactor sert deux objectifs à la fois.

## Défauts : les moins chers d'abord

**D1** (`ReportModal` tronque sur les octets → UTF-8 invalide) et **D6** (`wordWrap` mesure des octets) sont la même classe de bug, tous deux épinglés par des tests en `t.Skip()`, tous deux corrigeables en quelques lignes avec `runewidth`. **D3** (boucle infinie si `wrapWidth <= 0`) est un garde d'une ligne. Les trois tiennent dans une seule PR.

**D2** et **D4** demandent une décision de ta part, pas du code : D2 = soit verrouiller la checkbox, soit retirer l'affirmation du commentaire ; D4 = changer `Tab` en `↑/↓` casse la mémoire musculaire.

Par quoi je commence — la phase 1, le refactor `docker/client.go`, ou le lot de défauts UTF-8 ?
corrige le lot de défaut UTF-8, ensuite découpe
Je commence par le lot UTF-8 (D1, D6, D3), puis j'enchaîne sur le découpage.

| Helper | Use |
|---|---|
| `StringWidth` | column measurement, replaces `len()` on display values |
| `TruncateWidth` | keeps the head — titles, messages |
| `TruncateTailWidth` | keeps the tail — paths, where trailing segments identify the item |

  images.go      image ls, the system df -v scraper, rmi, pull, exposed ports
  networks.go    the docker network family, inspect, diagnostic containers

  launch.go      ContainerLaunchOptions and docker run argument building
  system.go      docker system df counters
  parse.go       size and NetIO parsing (already had a test file)

network.go became ports.go. It reports the host's own listening sockets by
running ss in a --net=host container and has nothing to do with Docker networks;
holding that name would have made networks.go actively misleading.

The seam is the point of the exercise. Every function called exec.Command
directly, which made the package untestable without a daemon and left it at
7.3 % coverage — the blocker the backlog recorded against phase 5. All calls now
pass through dockerRunner, whose one production implementation shells out as
before. dockerCmd carries the three variations that actually differ: stdin (for
`login --password-stdin`), whether stderr is merged (mutating calls surface it,
parsing calls do not), and whether the binary is docker or a credential helper.
Package-level dockerOutput/dockerCombined/mutate/prune wrappers keep the ~45
call sites terse.

grep for exec.Command outside exec.go now returns nothing: netdiag.go,
topology.go and ports.go were routed through the seam too, including two
LookPath sites that had drifted out of the pattern.

- registryCandidates, where Docker Hub's five aliases mean a wrong answer

- RegistryLogin, asserted to keep the password out of argv
- buildLaunchArgs: the image stays last, and empty form fields do not become
  empty arguments that make docker reject the run
- the unavailable-Docker paths of both dashboard counters, which must return a
  zero value rather than an error

Behaviour is unchanged except for two error strings in ports.go, which returned
a bare "docker not found" built with fmt.Errorf and no verb; they now wrap the
underlying error like every other call site.

# Plan Command

This command creates a comprehensive implementation plan before writing any code. It accepts either free-form requirements or a PRD markdown file.

Run inline by default. Do not call the Task tool or any subagent by default. This keeps `/plan` usable from plugin installs that ship commands without agent files.

## What This Command Does

1. **Restate Requirements** - Clarify what needs to be built
2. **Identify Risks** - Surface potential issues and blockers
3. **Create Step Plan** - Break down implementation into phases
4. **Wait for Confirmation** - MUST receive user approval before proceeding

## When to Use

Use `/plan` when:
- Starting a new feature
- Making significant architectural changes
- Working on complex refactoring
- Multiple files/components will be affected
- Requirements are unclear or ambiguous

## How It Works

The assistant will:

1. **Analyze the request** and restate requirements in clear terms
2. **Ground the plan** in relevant codebase patterns when the repo is available
3. **Break down into phases** with specific, actionable steps
4. **Identify dependencies** between components
5. **Assess risks** and potential blockers
6. **Estimate complexity** (High/Medium/Low)
7. **Present the plan** and WAIT for your explicit confirmation

## Input Modes

| Input | Mode | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `path/to/name.prd.md` | PRD artifact mode | Read the PRD, pick the next pending delivery milestone or implementation phase, and write `.claude/plans/{name}.plan.md` |
| Any other markdown path | Reference mode | Read the file as context and produce an inline plan |
| Free-form text | Conversational mode | Produce an inline plan |
| Empty input | Clarification mode | Ask what should be planned |

In PRD artifact mode, create `.claude/plans/` if needed. If the PRD contains a `Delivery Milestones` table, update only the selected row from `pending` to `in-progress` and set its `Plan` cell to the generated plan path. If the PRD uses the legacy `.claude/PRPs/prds/` format with `Implementation Phases`, read it without migrating paths.

## Pattern Grounding

Before writing the plan, search the codebase for conventions the implementation should mirror. Capture the top example for each relevant category with file references:

| Category | What to capture |
|---|---|
| Naming | File, function, type, command, or script naming in the affected area |
| Error handling | How failures are raised, returned, logged, or handled gracefully |
| Logging | Levels, format, and what gets logged |
| Data access | Repository, service, query, or filesystem patterns |
| Tests | Test file location, framework, fixtures, and assertion style |

If no similar code exists, state that explicitly. Do not invent a pattern.

## PRD Artifact Output

When called with a `.prd.md` file, write the plan to `.claude/plans/{kebab-case-name}.plan.md` using this structure:

````markdown
# Plan: {Feature Name}

**Source PRD**: {path}
**Selected Milestone**: {milestone or phase name}
**Complexity**: {Small | Medium | Large}

## Summary
{2-3 sentences}

## Patterns to Mirror
| Category | Source | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Naming | `path:line` | {short description} |
| Errors | `path:line` | {short description} |
| Tests | `path:line` | {short description} |

## Files to Change
| File | Action | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `path` | CREATE / UPDATE / DELETE | {reason} |

## Tasks
### Task 1: {name}
- **Action**: {what to do}
- **Mirror**: {pattern to follow}
- **Validate**: {command that proves correctness}

## Validation
```bash
{project-specific validation commands}
```

## Risks
| Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|

## Acceptance
- [ ] All tasks complete
- [ ] Validation passes
- [ ] Patterns mirrored, not reinvented
````

After writing the artifact, report its path and WAIT for confirmation before writing code.

## Example Usage

```
User: /plan I need to add real-time notifications when markets resolve

Assistant:
# Implementation Plan: Real-Time Market Resolution Notifications

## Requirements Restatement
- Send notifications to users when markets they're watching resolve
- Support multiple notification channels (in-app, email, webhook)
- Ensure notifications are delivered reliably
- Include market outcome and user's position result

## Implementation Phases

### Phase 1: Database Schema
- Add notifications table with columns: id, user_id, market_id, type, status, created_at
- Add user_notification_preferences table for channel preferences
- Create indexes on user_id and market_id for performance

### Phase 2: Notification Service
- Create notification service in lib/notifications.ts
- Implement notification queue using BullMQ/Redis
- Add retry logic for failed deliveries
- Create notification templates

### Phase 3: Integration Points
- Hook into market resolution logic (when status changes to "resolved")
- Query all users with positions in market
- Enqueue notifications for each user

### Phase 4: Frontend Components
- Create NotificationBell component in header
- Add NotificationList modal
- Implement real-time updates via Supabase subscriptions
- Add notification preferences page

## Dependencies
- Redis (for queue)
- Email service (SendGrid/Resend)
- Supabase real-time subscriptions

## Risks
- HIGH: Email deliverability (SPF/DKIM required)
- MEDIUM: Performance with 1000+ users per market
- MEDIUM: Notification spam if markets resolve frequently
- LOW: Real-time subscription overhead

## Estimated Complexity: MEDIUM
- Backend: 4-6 hours
- Frontend: 3-4 hours
- Testing: 2-3 hours
- Total: 9-13 hours

**WAITING FOR CONFIRMATION**: Proceed with this plan? (yes/no/modify)
```

## Important Notes

**CRITICAL**: This command will **NOT** write any code until you explicitly confirm the plan with "yes" or "proceed" or similar affirmative response.

If you want changes, respond with:
- "modify: [your changes]"
- "different approach: [alternative]"
- "skip phase 2 and do phase 3 first"

## Integration with Other Commands

After planning:
- Use the `tdd-workflow` skill to implement with test-driven development
- Use `/build-fix` if build errors occur
- Use `/code-review` to review completed implementation
- Use `/pr` or `/prp-pr` to open a pull request

> **Need requirements first?** Use `/plan-prd` for a lean PRD at `.claude/prds/{name}.prd.md`.
>
> **Need the legacy PRP flow?** Use `/prp-plan` for deep PRP planning with `.claude/PRPs/` artifacts. Use `/prp-implement` to execute those plans with rigorous validation loops.

## Optional Planner Agent

ECC also provides a `planner` agent for manual installs that include agent files. Use it only when the local runtime already exposes that subagent and the user explicitly asks you to delegate planning.

If the `planner` subagent is unavailable, continue planning inline instead of surfacing an "Agent type 'planner' not found" error.

For manual installs, the source file lives at:
`agents/planner.md`

## Le bug : l'isolation par contexte ne marche pas

Les trois méthodes encodent le contexte DevDesk dans le champ `path` du protocole credential de git :

```
protocol=https
host=gitlab.com
path=devdesk/context/prod     ← censé isoler les contextes
username=oauth2
password=<token>
```

Or git **ignore le `path` par défaut** : `credential.useHttpPath` vaut `false`, et git strippe le chemin avant de transmettre au helper. Vérifié à l'instant avec un store jetable :

```
approve  path=devdesk/context/default  password=TOKEN_DEFAULT
approve  path=devdesk/context/prod     password=TOKEN_PROD

$ cat creds
REDACTED     ← une seule entrée

$ git credential fill  (path=devdesk/context/default)
password=TOKEN_PROD                               ← le mauvais token
```

Conséquence concrète : deux contextes DevDesk pointant sur le même hôte GitLab **s'écrasent mutuellement**. Après `:context prod`, le contexte `default` renvoie le token de `prod`. Le stockage est en réalité clé par `protocol://host`, pas par contexte — et ça échoue silencieusement, sans erreur.

Ça touche tous les helpers (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), pas seulement `store` : le strip a lieu dans git lui-même, avant le helper.

Avec `useHttpPath = true`, ça marche comme prévu — deux entrées distinctes, bon token renvoyé. Mais c'est une config globale de l'utilisateur, que DevDesk ne pose nulle part et qui modifierait le comportement de git pour tous ses autres dépôts. Le vrai correctif est probablement d'encoder le contexte dans le `host` (`gitlab.com` → clé dérivée) ou dans le `username`, plutôt que dans un champ que git est libre de jeter.

## Défauts secondaires

- **`Delete` n'a pas de timeout** (`git_credential.go:160`) alors que `Save` et `Load` en ont un de 2 s. Le commentaire de `Save` explique pourquoi il est là : éviter que le TUI se fige si GCM n'est pas configuré ou attend une saisie. Le logout n'a pas cette protection.
- **Le timeout ne tue pas ce qu'il annonce.** Le commentaire dit « tuer le processus et tous ses enfants », mais `cmd.Process.Kill()` ne tue que le fils direct. GCM spawn un sous-processus qui survit.
- **`HelperStorage` (`helper.go`, 137 lignes) est du code mort** : construit nulle part hors de son propre fichier et d'un test. C'est `GitCredentialStorage` qui est câblé dans `internal/app/app.go`. Et il est buggé — `detectHelper()` peut renvoyer `store --file=/path`, que `"credential-"+helper` transforme en un seul argv `credential-store --file=/path`, introuvable. Il code aussi `protocol=https` en dur là où `GitCredentialStorage` parse le scheme.

## Ce que ça change pour les tests

La testabilité est en fait **moins** problématique que pour docker. Pas besoin de seam : `git credential` est entièrement pilotable par l'environnement.

```go
t.Setenv("GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL", filepath.Join(dir, "gitconfig"))  // helper = store --file=<tmp>
t.Setenv("GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM", "1")
```

C'est ce que je viens de faire à la main : hermétique, rapide, et ça ne touche pas le trousseau réel de l'utilisateur — ce qui serait inacceptable pour un test. On teste le vrai binaire git plutôt qu'un stub, donc on attrape des bugs comme celui du `path`, qu'un stub aurait au contraire figé dans le marbre.

Un seam resterait utile pour un seul cas : simuler le timeout sans attendre 2 s.

**Donc l'ordre logique s'inverse.** Écrire les tests d'abord graverait le comportement cassé. Je propose : corriger l'isolation de contexte, supprimer `helper.go`, puis couvrir. Found while planning the coverage work for `internal/credentials`. **Multi-context credential isolation has never worked.**

## The defect

All three methods carried the DevDesk context in the `path` field of the git credential protocol:

```
protocol=https
host=gitlab.com
path=devdesk/context/prod     ← meant to isolate contexts
username=oauth2
password=<token>
```

Git **discards the path field** unless `credential.useHttpPath` is set, and it defaults to off. Every credential was keyed on `protocol://host` alone.

Verified against a real credential store, before the fix:

```
approve  path=devdesk/context/default  password=TOKEN_DEFAULT
approve  path=devdesk/context/prod     password=TOKEN_PROD

$ cat .git-credentials
REDACTED      ← one entry, not two

$ git credential fill  (path=devdesk/context/default)
password=TOKEN_PROD                                ← the wrong token
```

So two contexts pointing at the same GitLab host overwrote each other, and the last one to authenticate won for all of them — silently, with no error surfaced anywhere.

This affects **every helper** (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), not just `store`: git strips the path before the helper is ever invoked.

## The fix

Pass `-c credential.useHttpPath=true` on each invocation.

Scoping it to the call is deliberate. Setting the option in the user's config would change how git resolves credentials for **every repository on their machine** — far beyond what DevDesk should be doing.

After the fix, same scenario:

```
$ cat .git-credentials
REDACTED
REDACTED
```

Each context loads its own token, and `reject` removes only the targeted entry.

⚠️ **Existing users must re-authenticate.** Credentials stored under the old path-stripped key no longer match. Those credentials were ambiguous across contexts anyway, so there is nothing meaningful to migrate.

## Two smaller defects went with it

- **`Delete` had no timeout**, while `Save` and `Load` bounded themselves to 2 s — precisely so an unconfigured helper could not freeze the TUI. Logout could hang indefinitely.
- **The timeout killed only the direct `git` child**, though the comment claimed it killed "le processus et tous ses enfants". The helper git spawns survives and holds the output pipes open, so `Run` kept blocking anyway.

The three calls now share one `runCredential` helper built on `exec.CommandContext` + `WaitDelay`. `WaitDelay` is what actually bounds the wait on those inherited pipes, and it replaces the goroutine-and-select dance that was duplicated twice.

## Deleted `helper.go`

`HelperStorage` (137 lines) was constructed nowhere outside its own tests — `GitCredentialStorage` is what `internal/app/app.go` wires in. It was also broken:

- `detectHelper()` returns whatever `git config credential.helper` holds. A common value like `store --file=/path` became the single argv element `credential-store --file=/path` — not a command that exists.
- It hardcoded `protocol=https`, unlike `GitCredentialStorage`, which reads the scheme from the URL.

No seam. `git credential` is fully steerable through the environment, so the tests redirect `HOME`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` and `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM` at a temp directory with a throwaway `store` helper. ## Ce qu'est un seam

Le terme vient de Michael Feathers (*Working Effectively with Legacy Code*). Un **seam** est un endroit où tu peux changer le comportement d'un programme **sans modifier le code à cet endroit**.

La métaphore est celle de la couture d'un vêtement : deux pièces sont jointes, et tu peux les séparer là sans découper le tissu.

### L'exemple du repo : `internal/docker`

Avant le découpage, chaque fonction appelait le CLI directement :

```go
func ListVolumes() ([]Volume, error) {
    output, err := exec.Command("docker", "volume", "ls", "--format", "...").Output()
    // ... parsing
}
```

L'appel à docker est **soudé** dans la fonction. Pour tester `ListVolumes`, il te faut un vrai démon Docker, avec de vrais volumes. Il n'existe aucun point où un test peut s'intercaler.

Ce qu'on a introduit dans `internal/docker/exec.go` :

```go
type dockerRunner interface {
    LookPath() error
    Run(cmd dockerCmd) ([]byte, error)
    Build(args ...string) *exec.Cmd
}

var runner dockerRunner = cliRunner{}   // ← le seam
```

`ListVolumes` appelle maintenant `dockerOutput(...)`, qui passe par `runner`. En production, `runner` est le vrai CLI. Dans un test, on le remplace par un stub qui renvoie une sortie figée. **Le code de `ListVolumes` n'a pas changé de comportement, et le test n'a rien édité** — il a juste basculé un point de décision.

Ce point de décision (ici, une variable de package) s'appelle l'**enabling point**. D'autres formes courantes : un paramètre de fonction, un champ d'interface sur un struct, une variable de fonction, un build tag.

### Pourquoi `gitlab` et `credentials` n'en avaient pas besoin

C'est le vrai enseignement des deux dernières PR. Un seam a un coût : une indirection, une interface qui n'existe que pour les tests. On n'en fabrique un que si le code n'offre **aucun point d'entrée naturel**.

| Package | Point d'entrée existant | Seam ? |
|---|---|---|
| `gitlab` | `NewClient(url, token)` — la base URL est déjà un enabling point, il suffit de la pointer sur `httptest` | non |
| `credentials` | `HOME`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` — git est **conçu** pour être piloté par l'environnement | non |
| `docker` | aucun : pas de variable d'environnement qui dise « parle à ce faux démon » et renvoie une sortie arbitraire | oui, fabriqué |

### Le piège du seam

Un stub te fait tester **ta** construction d'arguments et **ton** parsing — mais il encode aussi ton hypothèse sur ce que l'outil réel produit. Si l'hypothèse est fausse, le test passe et la production casse.

C'est exactement ce qui vient de se produire, à l'envers. Si j'avais mis un seam sur `git credential` et stubbé la réponse, le stub aurait fidèlement renvoyé le token du bon contexte — parce que c'est ce que je croyais que git faisait. Le test serait passé au vert, et le bug d'isolation serait resté. C'est en lançant le **vrai** binaire git que le comportement réel est apparu : git jette le champ `path`.

D'où la règle pratique : un seam quand la dépendance est trop coûteuse ou destructive à invoquer pour de vrai (un démon Docker, une API distante) ; le vrai outil quand il est rendable hermétique (git avec un `HOME` jetable). Ici c'était le cas, et ça a payé.

---

Sur la PR elle-même : deux défauts secondaires sont partis avec le principal — `Delete` n'avait pas de timeout alors que `Save` et `Load` en avaient un précisément pour éviter le gel du TUI, et le timeout ne tuait que le fils direct `git` alors que le commentaire prétendait le contraire (le helper survivant gardait les pipes ouverts, donc `Run` bloquait quand même). Les trois appels partagent maintenant un `runCredential` sur `exec.CommandContext` + `WaitDelay`.

À noter dans la PR : **les utilisateurs existants devront se réauthentifier**, les credentials stockés sous l'ancienne clé sans path ne correspondent plus.

Je n'ai pas mergé.
